In mathematics, the '''Lyapunov–Schmidt reduction''' or '''Lyapunov–Schmidt construction''' is used to study solutions to nonlinear equations in the case when the [[implicit function theorem]] does not work. It permits the reduction of infinite-dimensional equations in Banach spaces to finite-dimensional equations. It is named after [[Aleksandr Lyapunov]] and [[Erhard Schmidt]].

==Problem setup==
Let

:<math> f(x,\lambda)=0 \, </math>

be the given nonlinear equation,  <math> X,\Lambda, </math> and <math> Y </math> are
[[Banach space]]s (<math>\Lambda </math> is the [[parameter space]]). <math> f(x,\lambda) </math> is the
<math> C^p </math>-map from a neighborhood of some point <math> (x_0,\lambda_0)\in X\times \Lambda </math> to
<math> Y </math> and the equation is satisfied at this point

:<math> f(x_0,\lambda_0)=0. </math>

For the case when the linear operator <math> f_x(x,\lambda) </math> is invertible, the [[implicit function theorem]] assures that there exists
a solution <math> x(\lambda) </math> satisfying the equation <math> f(x(\lambda),\lambda)=0 </math> at least locally close to <math> \lambda_0 </math>.

In the opposite case, when the linear operator <math> f_x(x,\lambda) </math> is non-invertible, the Lyapunov–Schmidt reduction can be applied in the following
way.

==Assumptions==

One assumes that the operator  <math> f_x(x,\lambda) </math> is a [[Fredholm operator]], <math> \ker f_x (x_0,\lambda_0)=X_1, </math> and <math> X_1 </math> has finite dimension.

The [[range of a function|range]] of this operator <math> \mathrm{ran} f_x (x_0,\lambda_0)=Y_1 </math> has finite [[co-dimension]] and
is a closed subspace in <math> Y </math>.

[[Without loss of generality]], one can assume that <math> (x_0,\lambda_0)=(0,0). </math>

==Lyapunov–Schmidt construction==

Let us split  <math> X </math> and <math> Y </math> into the direct sums <math> X= X_1 \oplus X_2 </math> and <math> Y= Y_1 \oplus Y_2 </math>, respectively, where <math> \dim X_2, \dim Y_2 < \infty </math>. Also, let <math> Q </math> be the [[Projection (linear algebra)|projection operator]] onto  <math> Y_1 </math>.

Applying the operators <math> Q </math> and <math> I-Q </math> to the original  equation and writing <math> x = x_1 + x_2 </math>, one obtains the equivalent system

:<math> Qf(x_1 + x_2,\lambda)=0 \, </math>

:<math> (I-Q)f(x_1 + x_2,\lambda)=0 \, </math>

Viewing the first equation as a map

:<math> \psi: X_1 \times X_2 \times \Lambda \to Y_1</math>

where

:<math> \psi(x_1,x_2,\lambda) = Qf(x_1 + x_2,\lambda),</math>

one finds that <math> D_{x_2}\psi(0,0,0)[(0,x_2,0)] </math> is an isomorphism. The implicit function theorem is thus applicable, in particular guaranteeing the existence of a <math> x_2 = x_2(x_1,
\lambda) </math> such that

: <math> Qf(x_1 + x_2(x_1,\lambda),\lambda) = 0. </math>

Now plugging <math> x_2 = x_2(x_1,\lambda) </math> into the second equation, one obtains the [[Bifurcation theory|bifurcation equation]]

:<math> (I-Q)f(x_1+x_2(x_1,\lambda),\lambda)=0, \, </math>

which is a finite-dimensional equation by the earlier assumption of <math> \mathrm{codim} D_x f(0,0) </math> being finite. This equation is now to be solved with respect to <math> x_1 </math>, which is finite-dimensional, and parameters :<math> \lambda </math>

== Applications ==
Lyapunov–Schmidt reduction has been used in economics, natural sciences, and engineering<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Lyapunov-Schmidt methods in nonlinear analysis and applications|first=Nikolai|last=Sidorov|date=2011|publisher=Springer|isbn=9789048161508|oclc=751509629}}</ref> often in combination with [[bifurcation theory]], [[perturbation theory]], and [[Regularization (mathematics)|regularization]].<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Citation|last=Golubitsky|first=Martin|chapter=The Hopf Bifurcation|date=1985|title=Applied Mathematical Sciences|pages=337–396|publisher=Springer New York|isbn=9781461295334|last2=Schaeffer|first2=David G.|doi=10.1007/978-1-4612-5034-0_8}}</ref><ref name="Gupta 399–411">{{Cite journal|last=Gupta|first=Ankur|last2=Chakraborty|first2=Saikat|date=January 2009|title=Linear stability analysis of high- and low-dimensional models for describing mixing-limited pattern formation in homogeneous autocatalytic reactors|journal=Chemical Engineering Journal|volume=145|issue=3|pages=399–411|doi=10.1016/j.cej.2008.08.025|issn=1385-8947}}</ref> LS reduction is often used to rigorously regularize [[partial differential equation]] models in [[chemical engineering]] resulting in models that are easier to simulate [[Numerical partial differential equations|numerically]] but still retain all the parameters of the original model.<ref name="Gupta 399–411"/><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Balakotaiah|first=Vemuri|date=March 2004|title=Hyperbolic averaged models for describing dispersion effects in chromatographs and reactors|journal=Korean Journal of Chemical Engineering|volume=21|issue=2|pages=318–328|doi=10.1007/bf02705415|issn=0256-1115}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Gupta|first=Ankur|last2=Chakraborty|first2=Saikat|date=2008-01-19|title=Dynamic Simulation of Mixing-Limited Pattern Formation in Homogeneous Autocatalytic Reactions|journal=Chemical Product and Process Modeling|volume=3|issue=2|doi=10.2202/1934-2659.1135|issn=1934-2659}}</ref>
